name: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH, Forestier disease)

clinicalPearls: A non-inflammatory condition characterised by flowing ossification along the anterolateral aspect of the vertebral bodies, likened to 'flowing candle wax'
Diagnosis classically requires flowing ossification bridging at least four contiguous vertebrae with preservation of the intervertebral disc spaces
The sacroiliac joints and apophyseal (facet) joints are preserved, which helps distinguish it from ankylosing spondylitis
Most common in older men and strongly associated with metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes and obesity
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can cause spinal stiffness, reduced range of movement and, when cervical, dysphagia from anterior osteophytes
Enthesopathy with new bone at extraspinal sites (heels, pelvis, elbows) is common
Management is largely symptomatic with analgesia and physiotherapy, and surgery is reserved for complications such as severe dysphagia or myelopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is a non-inflammatory ossifying diathesis in which new bone is laid down at entheses and along the spine, particularly the anterolateral vertebral margins, through progressive endochondral and membranous ossification. The disc spaces, sacroiliac joints and facet joints remain intact, distinguishing it from inflammatory spondyloarthropathy. Metabolic factors are strongly implicated: hyperinsulinaemia, insulin-like growth factor and other growth-promoting mediators associated with metabolic syndrome, diabetes and obesity are thought to stimulate osteoblast activity and enthesial new bone formation. The accumulating anterior bridging osteophytes stiffen the spine and, in the cervical region, can mechanically impinge on the oesophagus and airway.
additionalInvestigations: Spinal radiographs demonstrating flowing anterolateral ossification over four or more vertebrae with preserved discs
CT of the spine to characterise the extent of ossification and cervical osteophytes
Barium swallow or endoscopy when cervical osteophytes cause dysphagia
Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile to assess associated metabolic syndrome
MRI if spinal canal stenosis, myelopathy or ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament is suspected
redFlags: Progressive dysphagia or airway compromise from large cervical osteophytes
Neurological deficit suggesting myelopathy or associated spinal canal stenosis
Unstable spinal fracture through an ankylosed, brittle segment after minor trauma
New severe pain that could indicate fracture, infection or malignancy in a stiff spine
reference.prognosis: DISH is generally benign and slowly progressive; many patients remain asymptomatic, but spinal ankylosis increases fracture risk after minor trauma and large osteophytes can occasionally cause dysphagia or neurological compromise.
pitfalls: Confusing DISH with ankylosing spondylitis and missing the preserved discs and sacroiliac joints
Underestimating fracture risk in the rigid, brittle ankylosed spine after minor trauma
Overlooking cervical osteophytes as a cause of unexplained dysphagia
Failing to assess and manage the associated metabolic syndrome
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for spinal stiffness and enthesopathic pain, as there is no disease-modifying drug therapy
Physiotherapy and structured exercise to preserve spinal mobility, posture and range of movement
Aggressive management of the associated metabolic syndrome, with weight reduction, glycaemic control of type 2 diabetes and lipid optimisation
Soft-diet modification and referral for surgical osteophytectomy when cervical anterior osteophytes cause dysphagia or airway compromise
Heightened vigilance for unstable fractures of the ankylosed rigid spine after even minor trauma, with a low threshold for CT and spinal immobilisation
Surgical decompression for spinal canal stenosis, myelopathy or ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
Multidisciplinary referral involving rheumatology, ENT or gastroenterology and spinal surgery as manifestations dictate
